previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with chest pain and a cough. The chest pain occurred both with coughing and exertion. Evaluation ruled out acute myocardial infarction, with normal cardiac enzymes and a normal exercise stress MIBI test. The cough was attributed to acute bronchitis, with improvement after IV fluids. A dental Panorex revealed radiolucency at tooth #21, concerning for infection, and the patient was started on penicillin. Chronic conditions including coronary artery disease, diabetes, hypertension, and diastolic heart failure were managed with medication adjustments. The patient was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with dentistry and monitor weight and symptoms.

Brief Hospital Course: The patient is a ___ year old male with a history of CAD s/p multiple past PCIs, who presented with chest pain starting the evening of ___ and increasing over the next day until peaking the morning of admission. A recent cardiac perfusion study on ___ showed an EF of 54%. His Troponin was <0.01 when measured in the ED. CXR showed mild left basilar atelectasis but was otherwise normal. The pain appears to be musculoskeletal in origin, with tenderness to palpation over the chest wall. By the time of discharge, it was no longer present unless exacerbated by coughing. . # Coronary Artery Disease: The patient has a significant history of CAD, with multiple episodes of stent restenosis. The timing of his symptoms is concerning for crescendo angina, but other details of the presentation are not typical of anginal pain. On exam, the chest pain was reproducible by palpation of the chest wall and worsened by coughing. His cardiac enzymes were negative and his EKG showed normal sinus rhythm without evidence of new ischemia, making ACS very unlikely. While admitted, he was kept on telemetry without any concerning events noted. His home cardiac regimen of full dose Aspirin, Clopidogrel, and Atorvastatin were continued. . # Chest Pain: Possible etiologies for his chest pain include ACS, PE, pneumothorax, musculoskeletal pain, and pneumonia. CXR on admission showed no evidence of pneumothorax, but did show mild left basilar atelectasis. His history of left leg injury in ___ and current calf tenderness was worrisome for DVT and possible PE, but a venous doppler study was negative for DVT. The worsening of his pain with cough is very suggestive of a musculoskeletal or pleural process. The reproducibility of the pain with palpation of the anterior chest also suggests a musculoskeletal process. The patient cannot tolerate NSAIDs due to his GI issues, but the pain did improve somewhat with Tylenol. Cough suppression brought him near full relieve by the time of discharge. Warm packs were also recommended. . # Cough: The patient reports a non productive cough over the last few days. He remained afebrile and a CXR on admission showed only mild atelectasis at the left lung base. His WBC count was somewhat low at 3.8, but this is not particularly worrisome without other findings. There is no evidence for pneumonia. The cough is most likely due to a mild viral infection, particularly given his development of malaise and diffuse, mild myalgias after admission. However, since the cough is exacerbating his chest pain, it should be controlled. He was given Guaifenesin and Codeine with near complete improvement of symptoms. -- Guaifenesin ___ mL PO/NG Q6H:PRN cough -- Codeine Sulfate ___ mg PO/NG Q4H:PRN cough . # Diabetes: His home diabetes regimen includes Metformin 850 mg PO BID and Pioglitazone 45 mg PO daily. These were held while admitted. He is also on fixed insulin doses of Humalog Mix (75-25) at home, which were continued along with a Humalog sliding scale. His fingerstick glucose levels remained stable. . # Hyperlipidemia: We continued his home Atorvastatin 80 mg PO daily. . # Hypertension: While admitted, he was given Metoprolol Tartrate instead of Metoprolol Succinate at equivalent doses. Based on the blood pressures observed, his daily dose of Metoprolol was increased from 150 mg to 200 mg. His Valsartan 40 mg PO daily was continued. . # Hypothyroidism: His Levothyroxine 100 mcg PO daily was continued while admitted. His TSH was 5.5 on ___, several days before admission, which is somewhat elevated. On the morning of discharge, however, his TSH was 1.6, suggesting that he may not have been compliant with his medication at home. . # GERD / Constipation: The patient has a significant history of reflux and constipation. He was recently seen in clinic for complaints of worsening symptoms. He was continued on his extensive home bowel regimen in the hospital. The only change was a decreased dose of Ranitidine from 300 mg BID to ___ mg BID at the recommendation of the pharmacist. His hypothyroidism may be contributing to his GI issues, and he would likely benefit from better control of his thyroid hormone levels. . # NASH: A liver panel sent on ___ was relatively normal and similar to his prior baseline with ALT 38, AST 25, ALK 86, and TBili 0.7. No signs of acutely worsening hepatic function were noted during his stay. .
